1.title: Choose a Data Store
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Choose a Data Store. This module covers the task statement: choose a data store. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Match a workload to a store: Redshift, DynamoDB, R D S (Relational Database Service) and Aurora, S three, E M R (Elastic MapReduce), Lake Formation, MemoryDB, Neptune, DocumentDB, Keyspaces, OpenSearch, Kinesis and M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka). Configure each store for its access pattern, cost and performance. Use vector indexes (H N S W, I V F (inverted file)) and MemoryDB for fast lookups and similarity search. Integrate migration tools such as A W S Transfer Family. Use Redshift federated queries, materialized views and Spectrum for remote access. Manage locks and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Picks Its Stores
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Picks Its Stores. Raw telemetry and files need cheap, durable storage. Invoices need relational integrity and joins. Live truck status must be read in milliseconds by key. Analysts run heavy aggregate reports over years of data. Search over delivery notes and a "similar issues" feature. Your job: one workload, one store, with the right settings.

1.title: Matching the Workload to the Store
1.text: Matching the Workload to the Store. The figure shows this: Choosing a data store: S three for the lake, Redshift for analytics, DynamoDB for key-value, R D S or Aurora for relational, MemoryDB for in-memory, Neptune for graph, DocumentDB for documents, Keyspaces for Cassandra, OpenSearch for search and vectors.

1.title: Matching the Workload to the Store, continued
1.text: Matching the Workload to the Store, continued. Amazon S three. Model and strength: Object storage, eleven nines durability, cheap, any format. Pick it when: Data lake, raw and curated zones, archives, files for Athena, E M R, Glue. Amazon Redshift. Model and strength: Columnar M P P (massively parallel processing) data warehouse (S Q L, O L A P (online analytical processing)). Pick it when: Heavy analytics and B I (business intelligence) over large structured data; joins and aggregates. Amazon DynamoDB. Model and strength: Key-value and document, serverless, single-digit millisecond at any scale. Pick it when: Known access patterns by key, high write rates, spiky traffic. Amazon R D S or Aurora. Model and strength: Relational O L T P (online transaction processing) (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, S Q L Server; Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible). Pick it when: Transactions, joins, referential integrity, existing S Q L apps.

1.title: Matching the Workload to the Store, continued
1.text: Matching the Workload to the Store, continued. Amazon MemoryDB. Model and strength: Durable in-memory database, Valkey and Redis O S S (open source software) compatible, microsecond reads, single-digit millisecond writes, Multi-A Z (Availability Zone) transaction log. Pick it when: Primary database for ultra-fast key or value, session, leaderboard, vector data; no separate cache needed. Amazon Neptune. Model and strength: Graph database (property graph and R D F (Resource Description Framework)). Pick it when: Highly connected data: fraud rings, recommendations, knowledge graphs, lineage. Amazon DocumentDB. Model and strength: Document database, MongoDB-compatible. Pick it when: Existing MongoDB workloads, flexible Jason documents. Amazon Keyspaces. Model and strength: Apache Cassandra-compatible, serverless wide-column. Pick it when: Existing Cassandra workloads. Amazon OpenSearch Service. Model and strength: Search and analytics engine, log analytics, k N N vector search. Pick it when: Full-text search, log and event analysis, semantic search.

1.title: Matching the Workload to the Store, continued
1.text: Matching the Workload to the Store, continued. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or M S K. Model and strength: Streams with retention. Pick it when: Replayable event logs (Module two). Amazon E M R (H D F S) or E B S (Elastic Block Store) or E F S (Elastic File System). Model and strength: Cluster file system or block or shared file. Pick it when: Transient cluster storage; shared files; prefer S three for durable data. A W S Lake Formation. Model and strength: Governed data lake on S three and the Glue catalog. Pick it when: Central permissions and cataloging for the lake (Modules seven and fifteen). Exam tip: The access pattern decides: ad-hoc S Q L over huge data to Redshift (or Athena on S three); lookups by key at massive scale to DynamoDB; transactions and joins to R D S or Aurora; cheap durable storage of anything to S three.

1.title: Amazon Redshift configuration
1.text: Amazon Redshift configuration. Provisioned (R A three nodes with managed storage that separates compute from storage) or Redshift Serverless (scales automatically, pay for use, good for spiky or unpredictable workloads). Distribution style decides how rows spread over slices: auto (default, Redshift chooses), even (round robin; no joins or unclear), key (same key on the same slice: co-locate joined tables), all (a full copy on every node: small, rarely changing dimension tables). Sort keys order rows on disk so range filters skip blocks: compound (leading column first) or auto; automatic table optimization can tune them.

1.title: Amazon Redshift configuration, continued
1.text: Amazon Redshift configuration, continued. Concurrency scaling and workload management (W L M) keep many users responsive; materialized views speed repeated queries. Load with copy, unload with unload (Module eight).

1.title: Amazon DynamoDB configuration
1.text: Amazon DynamoDB configuration. Capacity modes: on-demand (pay per request; unpredictable traffic) or provisioned (set read and write capacity; predictable traffic, with auto scaling). Primary key: a partition key (and optional sort key) that spreads load evenly; avoid a hot partition. Secondary indexes: global (G S I) (any key, own capacity, eventually consistent) and local (L S I) (same partition key, different sort key, created with the table). Dax (DynamoDB Accelerator) is a managed cache in front of DynamoDB for microsecond reads; T T L (time to live), streams and point-in-time recovery (Module eight).

1.title: RDS and Aurora configuration
1.text: R D S and Aurora configuration. Instance class and storage type for the workload; Multi-A Z for high availability; read replicas for read scaling; Aurora shares one cluster volume across up to fifteen replicas and offers Aurora Serverless version two. Use R D S Proxy to pool connections from Lambda and other bursty clients.

1.title: Amazon EMR and Lake Formation
1.text: Amazon E M R and Lake Formation. E M R: use S three as the durable store and H D F S (Hadoop Distributed File System) only for temporary shuffle or hot data; choose instance fleets with Spot. Lake Formation adds fine-grained permissions and cataloging to the S three lake.

1.title: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types
1.text: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types. A vector is a list of numbers (an embedding) that represents the meaning of text, an image or a record; similar items have nearby vectors. A vector store keeps embeddings and finds the nearest neighbors (k N N) by cosine similarity, Euclidean distance or inner product. Where vectors live: Aurora PostgreSQL and R D S for PostgreSQL (the pgvector extension), Amazon OpenSearch Service (k N N plugin, knn vector fields), Amazon MemoryDB (vector search in memory), Amazon DocumentDB and Neptune Analytics; knowledge bases for Amazon Bedrock can use Aurora PostgreSQL, OpenSearch and other stores.

1.title: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types, continued
1.text: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types, continued. The figure shows this: Vector index types: H N S W (Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds) uses layered neighbor graphs for fast, high-recall search at a higher memory cost; I V F uses clusters so a query searches only the nearest few.

1.title: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types, continued
1.text: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types, continued. H N S W (Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds). How it works: A layered graph of neighbors; a search hops from a coarse layer down to the nearest points. Trade-offs: High recall and fast queries, no training step; more memory and slower to build. I V F (inverted file, IVFFlat in pgvector). How it works: Vectors are grouped into clusters (centroids); a search checks only the nearest few clusters (probes). Trade-offs: Faster to build, less memory; recall depends on the number of clusters and probes; needs data present to build. Exact (no index). How it works: Compares every vector. Trade-offs: Perfect recall, slow for large sets.

1.title: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types, continued
1.text: Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types, continued. Both are approximate nearest neighbor (A N N) indexes: they trade a little recall (accuracy) for much lower latency. pgvector zero point five.zero or later supports H N S W indexes on Aurora PostgreSQL.

1.title: Amazon MemoryDB for fast key/value access
1.text: Amazon MemoryDB for fast key or value access. All data in memory, microsecond reads, single-digit millisecond writes, durable across multiple A Zs by a transaction log: unlike a cache, it can be the system of record. Use for session state, real-time leaderboards, rate limits and low-latency feature or vector lookups. Exam tip: "Similarity search in an existing PostgreSQL database" to Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and an H N S W index. "Durable microsecond key or value store" to MemoryDB. "Faster index build and lower memory, lower recall acceptable" to I V F.

1.title: AWS Transfer Family
1.text: A W S Transfer Family. Managed file transfer into and out of S three and E F S over S F T P (Secure File Transfer Protocol), F T P S (File Transfer Protocol Secure), F T P (File Transfer Protocol) and A S two (Applicability Statement two); no servers to run. Use when partners or legacy systems send files by S F T P; files land in S three and can trigger event-driven ingestion (Module one). Related tools: A W S DataSync (managed online transfer), A W S D M S (Database Migration Service) (databases), A W S Snow Family (offline), Application Discovery Service and Application Migration Service (servers and applications).

2.title: Redshift remote access
2.text: Redshift remote access. Redshift Spectrum. What it does: Query files in S three through external tables (Glue Data Catalog) without loading them; processing happens in the Spectrum layer. Pick it when: Cold or huge data stays in S three, joined with warehouse tables. Federated query. What it does: Query live data in R D S or Aurora (PostgreSQL, MySQL) from Redshift. Pick it when: Join operational data with the warehouse without E T L (extract, transform, load). Materialized view. What it does: Stores the precomputed result of a query; refresh automatically or manually; can be built over external and streaming sources. Pick it when: Repeated expensive queries, dashboards, streaming ingestion. Data sharing. What it does: Share live data between Redshift clusters or accounts. Pick it when: Module eighteen.

2.title: Redshift remote access, continued
2.text: Redshift remote access, continued. copy or unload. What it does: Load from and write to S three. Pick it when: Module eight. Exam tip: "Query historical files in S three from Redshift without loading them" to Redshift Spectrum. "Join live Aurora data with warehouse tables, no pipeline" to federated query. "Speed up the same heavy dashboard query" to materialized view.

2.title: Locks
2.text: Locks. A lock stops other sessions from changing (or reading) data while a transaction is using it, so results stay consistent. Amazon Redshift: each statement auto-commits unless you use begin or end; readers see the latest committed snapshot and do not wait for writers; concurrent writes to the same table can queue or fail with a serializable isolation error; truncate and vacuum commit open transactions; find sessions and locks in system views (for example S T V locks) and end a blocking session (P G terminate backend).

2.title: Locks, continued
2.text: Locks, continued. Amazon R D S and Aurora: the engine uses row and table locks; long transactions hold locks and cause lock waits and deadlocks (the engine rolls back one victim); use short transactions, consistent access order, and select... for update only where needed. Prevent problems: keep transactions short, commit promptly, schedule heavy loads away from reports, and retry after a deadlock or serialization error. DynamoDB has no row locks: use conditional writes, transactions and optimistic locking with a version attribute. Exam tip: "A Redshift load blocks other statements" or "deadlock" to find the blocking session in the lock system views, keep transactions short and retry.

2.title: Open Table Formats and Amazon S3 Tables
2.text: Open Table Formats and Amazon S three Tables. A table format adds table-level metadata on top of data files in S three so engines treat them as real tables. Apache Iceberg (also Apache Hudi and Delta Lake) gives A C I D (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) transactions, schema evolution, partition evolution, time travel (query or roll back to an earlier snapshot), row-level updates and deletes and hidden partitioning. Iceberg works with Athena, A W S Glue, Amazon E M R, Amazon Redshift and Apache Spark, with the Glue Data Catalog as the catalog. Maintenance for self-managed Iceberg: compact small files, expire old snapshots, remove orphan files.

2.title: Open Table Formats and Amazon S3 Tables, continued
2.text: Open Table Formats and Amazon S three Tables, continued. Amazon S three Tables are table buckets that store Apache Iceberg tables natively with automatic compaction, snapshot management and unreferenced-file removal, higher transactions per second than self-managed tables, access control in the S three tables namespace and integration with the Glue Data Catalog; query with Athena, Redshift, E M R, Spark and Quick. Exam tip: "Row-level updates and deletes and time travel on a data lake in S three" to Apache Iceberg. "Iceberg tables without managing compaction" to Amazon S three Tables.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Workload to store: S three lake; Redshift O L A P; DynamoDB key-value; R D S or Aurora O L T P; MemoryDB durable in-memory; Neptune graph; DocumentDB MongoDB. Redshift: R A three managed storage or Serverless; diststyle auto or even or key or all; sort keys. DynamoDB: On-demand versus provisioned; partition key spreads load; G S I (global secondary index) versus L S I (local secondary index); Dax cache. R D S or Aurora: Multi-A Z, read replicas, Aurora up to fifteen replicas, Serverless version two, R D S Proxy. Vectors: pgvector (Aurora or R D S PostgreSQL), OpenSearch k N N, MemoryDB. Transfer: Transfer Family (S F T P or F T P S or F T P or A S two to S three or E F S), DataSync, D M S, Snow Family. Locks: Redshift snapshots for readers, S T V locks, short transactions, retry; R D S row locks and deadlocks. Open tables: Iceberg (A C I D, evolution, time travel), S three Tables (managed Iceberg, auto compaction).

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Kestrel Freight's analysts run complex aggregate queries with joins across five years of structured shipment data and need the best price-performance for repeated B I reports. Which store fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Redshift is a columnar M P P data warehouse built for heavy analytic S Q L. DynamoDB is for key-based access and Keyspaces for Cassandra workloads.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A truck-status service must read the latest position by truck I D in single-digit milliseconds at very high scale with spiky traffic and no capacity planning. What should the engineer choose? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. DynamoDB on-demand serves key lookups at low latency and scales with spiky traffic without capacity planning.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. A team needs similarity search over embeddings stored in an existing Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database, with fast queries and high recall. Which two choices apply? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. pgvector adds the vector type and similarity operators, and an H N S W index gives fast approximate nearest-neighbor search with high recall. The other options do not provide vector search.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A company stores years of rarely queried files in S three and wants Redshift users to query them together with warehouse tables without loading them. Which feature should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Spectrum queries files in S three through external tables without loading them and can join them with local tables. Federated query is for live R D S or Aurora data.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A data lake in S three needs row-level updates and deletes, schema evolution and the ability to query earlier snapshots. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Iceberg adds A C I D transactions, row-level changes, schema evolution and time travel on top of files in S three.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which statement about distribution styles in Amazon Redshift is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. all copies the whole table to every node, which suits small slowly changing tables. key co-locates matching values, even is round robin, and auto lets Redshift choose.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A durable, in-memory database is needed as the primary store for session data, with microsecond reads and Multi-A Z durability. Which service should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. MemoryDB is a durable in-memory database compatible with Valkey and Redis O S S, with microsecond reads and a Multi-A Z transaction log.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Partners deliver files by S F T P every day, and the company wants them in S three without running servers. Which service should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Transfer Family provides managed S F T P, F T P S and F T P endpoints that write into S three or E F S.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: D. Question two: A. Question three: B and E. Question four: C. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: A. Question eight: D. In the next module, we continue the course.
